notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 18:24–46, drawn from the pages I was able to access. I have noted where I could not locate material on a particular point.

---

## Verse 24

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah proposed a public test: both sides would call upon their deity, and the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. The people immediately agreed, seeing it as a fair and decisive way to settle the dispute.

- **Ellicott** notes that a “sign from heaven” by fire was not unfamiliar in Israel’s history (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Chronicles 21:26; 2 Chronicles 7:1). He adds that such a sign, though not to be demanded as a ground of faith (Matthew 12:38–39), was granted by God when needed to startle an ignorant and misguided people. He observes that since Baal was worshipped as a nature-god (perhaps the sun), the miracle entered the very sphere Baal supposedly controlled, reclaiming it for Yahweh. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Gill** comments that the people’s response — “It is well spoken” — indicates they considered it a very reasonable proposal and a good method to determine who was the true God. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** highlights that Elijah gave the prophets of Baal every advantage: they could choose which bull to sacrifice, and they would pray first. He also notes that it was thought Baal was the sky-god and lord of lightning (fire from the sky), so if Baal were real, he certainly could send fire. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verses 25–26

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah told the prophets of Baal to go first, since they were so numerous. They took the bull, prepared it, and called on Baal from morning until noon. There was no answer; they leaped (or danced) around the altar.

- **Gill** notes that the prophets agreed (perhaps by silence). He cites a rabbinic opinion that they thought Baal (associated with the sun or Mars, a fiery planet) could send fire. He also notes the vivid description: “no voice, nor any that answered.” Their leaping around the altar was either a customary ritual dance or a mark of frenzy; the Targum renders it “they were mad on it.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Ellicott** describes the repeated cry “O Baal, hear us” as probably first a measured chant that degenerated into a wild, excited cry — an illustration of our Lord’s words about the heathen who “think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Matthew 6:7). He notes the grave irony in the blank silence: “There was no voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** observes that the prophets of Baal had a devoted and energetic prayer life — long, passionate, and enthusiastic — yet because it was not directed to the real God, it meant nothing. He comments: “There was no voice; no one answered.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that the Hebrew verb translated “leaped” is the same word translated “halt” (or “falter”) in verse 21. Gesenius thought it was used scornfully of the awkward dancing of the priests, but the Pulpit editors think it simply describes the reeling, swaying, bacchantic dance, comparable to that of dancing dervishes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-18.html)

---

## Verse 27

**Traditional Reading:** At noon Elijah began to mock the prophets. His taunts were sharp and sarcastic — “Shout louder, for he is a god! Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey, or sleeping and must be awakened.”

- **Ellicott** says the mockery is “the bitter irony of sheer contempt,” calling Baal a god only to heap upon him ideas most ungodlike: busy, in retirement, far away, or asleep in the noonday heat. He explains that in this crisis of conflict, there was no room for the kind of gentle appreciation Paul later showed at Athens (Acts 17:22–23); this was a battle between spiritual worship and a foul, cruel idolatry, and the case was not heathen ignorance but Israel’s apostasy. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Gill** notes that the words “meditating” or “pursuing” (busy) can, according to Rabbi S. Jarchi, carry a very coarse meaning: “Perhaps he has gone to a private place to relieve himself.” This reduces Baal to the lowest contempt. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** adds that Patterson and Austel comment that Elijah’s “irony bordered on sarcasm,” and that the words translated “meditating” and “busy” may be a euphemism for bodily elimination. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verse 28

**Traditional Reading:** The prophets shouted louder and, as was their custom, cut themselves with knives and lances until blood gushed over them.

- **Ellicott** explains that self-mutilation was common in Oriental frenzy, possibly a portion or survival of human sacrifice — the notion that self-torture and shedding of human blood would win divine favour. He adds that this delusion is “not confined to heathen religions, though excusable only in them.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** cites Wiseman, who notes that the practice of self-inflicted wounds to arouse a deity’s pity is attested at Ugarit, where men “bathed in their own blood like an ecstatic prophet.” Guzik observes that the prophets were utterly sincere and completely devoted — they had zeal, but without knowledge. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verse 29

**Traditional Reading:** Midday passed and they kept on “raving” (or “prophesying”) until the time of the evening sacrifice. Still no response — no one answered, no one paid attention.

- **Ellicott** notes that the Hebrew verb for “prophesied” here means they raved in their frenzy — comparable to Saul in his hour of madness (1 Samuel 18:10). He contrasts this with true prophetic inspiration, which, even when overmastering the will, gave no place to frenzy; “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** summarizes the sad result of worshipping an imaginary god: “We may dedicate great sincerity, sacrifice, and devotion to such gods, but it means nothing. There is no one there to answer.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verse 30

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah called the people to draw near. He then repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down.

- **Ellicott** notes that the altar of the LORD is “evidently referred to as well known, and here accepted by Elijah as having a true sacredness.” He explains that the exclusive consecration of the Jerusalem sanctuary, if ever thoroughly recognised, was now broken down by the religious severance of Israel. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** says Elijah wanted to get the people’s attention for their own benefit, so they would see that the LORD was the true God. He observes that Elijah was repairing something that once stood strong — there was once an altar at Carmel; Elijah was reviving something that had been. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Keathley (Bible.org, evangelical)** sees the repair of the altar as depicting “coming to the Lord on His terms by repentance or confession, and restoring the areas of access we have neglected.” He notes that the Hebrew word for offering a sacrifice, *qarab*, meant “to come near, approach, draw near.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

---

## Verse 31

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD had come saying, “Israel shall be your name.”

- **Ellicott** says the emphatic notice of the twelve stones is significant: “In spite of political division, and even religious separation, the tribes were still united in the covenant of God.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** reiterates the same point: the twelve stones represented the unity of the covenant people despite the political split between the northern and southern kingdoms. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verse 32

**Traditional Reading:** With the stones Elijah built an altar in the name of the LORD, and dug a trench around it large enough to hold two seahs of seed.

- **Ellicott** explains that a “seah” (measure) was the third part of an ephah, less than three gallons. A trench to hold only about six gallons seems too small for the context; therefore he suggests the sense is “large enough for the sowing (as in a furrow) of two measures of seed.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** does not comment at length on the trench size but notes it as part of Elijah’s careful preparation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verses 33–35

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah arranged the wood, cut up the bull, placed it on the wood, and then commanded that four waterpots be filled and poured over the offering and the wood — not once, but three times. The water ran down around the altar and filled the trench.

- **Guzik** says that by drenching the sacrifice three times, Elijah “showed more faith in God than he demanded from Baal — confident it was no harder for the Lord to ignite a wet sacrifice than a dry one.” He cites Wiseman’s comment that there could be “no question of trickery, such as the use of naptha instead of water, or mirrors for ignition.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Ellicott** explains that during a drought, getting so much water naturally raised questions. Josephus records that water was drawn from a perennial spring near the traditional site of the sacrifice, which never fails even in the severest drought. This precluded all idea of fraud. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keathley (Bible.org)** applies this spiritually: “Do our lives give unmistakable evidence of the power of God, or are we building fires under our sacrifices?” (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

---

## Verses 36–37

**Traditional Reading:** At the time of the evening sacrifice, Elijah prayed: “O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command. Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again.”

- **Guzik** notes that Elijah still remembered the evening sacrifice prescribed at the Jerusalem temple, even though Jeroboam had officially severed the northern kingdom from that worship some 50 years earlier. He observes that Elijah’s prayer was simple and focused on four things: (1) that God be known as God in Israel, (2) that Elijah be known as God’s servant, (3) that all was done at God’s word, and (4) that the people’s hearts be turned back. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Ellicott** emphasizes the name “JEHOVAH” thrice repeated in this short prayer. He says Elijah desired to efface himself: the God of Israel is the true worker, not only in the outer sphere by miracle but in the inner sphere by converting hearts. He calls Elijah, like his New Testament antitype John the Baptist, “but a voice calling on men ‘to prepare the way of the Lord.’” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keathley (Bible.org)** elaborates: “Elijah’s confidence in prayer was based on the revelation of the character and nature of God as Yahweh, and on the specific principles and plan of God as revealed in the covenants of promise.” He stresses that Elijah was acting according to the revelation of Scripture — “He was standing on the promises!” (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

- **Precept Austin** notes that the prayer was “simple, short, and sincere” and that Elijah urged a fourfold reason for the miracle: (1) that God be known as God, (2) that Elijah be known as God’s servant, (3) that all was done at God’s word, (4) that the people’s hearts be turned back. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary)

---

## Verse 38

**Traditional Reading:** The fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, and licked up the water in the trench.

- **Guzik** remarks that the fire consumed not only the sacrifice but also the wood, stones, dust, and water — going “beyond what was needed for vindication and instead glorifying Himself before all the people.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Precept Austin** calls this “a Pentecostal day for Israel” and laments that “it is because of our unbelief that signs and wonders are not still being wrought among us.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary)

---

## Verse 39

**Traditional Reading:** When the people saw it, they fell facedown and cried, “The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!”

- **Ellicott** draws a parallel to Leviticus 9:24, when fire from heaven inaugurated the Tabernacle sacrifices, noting the characteristic addition of the cry, “Jehovah; He, and He only, is God.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** offers a sobering caution: “The people’s recognition … was a momentary persuasion, not a lasting revival — a sobering reminder that even spectacular miracles don’t guarantee permanent change of heart.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Verse 40

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah ordered the people to seize the prophets of Baal, not letting one escape. They brought them down to the Kishon Valley and slaughtered them there.

- **Ellicott** addresses the moral difficulty directly: “This ruthless slaughter … belongs alike to the fierce righteousness of the character of Elijah, and to the spirit of the old Law (Deuteronomy 13:6–18; 17:2–7).” He explains that the law was adapted to the “hardness of men’s hearts,” not yet recognising the distinction between moral/political offences and religious sin that we leave to God’s judgment. He adds that the Baal prophets were likely implicated in Jezebel’s persecution of Yahweh’s prophets, and that the Baal-worship was “a licentious and perhaps bloody system.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keil & Delitzsch** say Elijah acted “not so much from revenge … as to carry out the fundamental law of the Old Testament kingdom of God, which prohibited idolatry on pain of death, and commanded that false prophets should be destroyed (Deuteronomy 17:2–3; Deuteronomy 13:13).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-18.html)

- **Guzik** does not dwell on the ethics but simply recounts the event as obedience to God’s command in Exodus 22:20. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

*(Note: I was unable to fetch a distinct Catholic/Orthodox reading on this verse, though Catholic commentaries typically note that the Church does not endorse such execution today, seeing it as belonging to the Old Covenant’s temporal sanctions.)*

---

## Verse 41

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah told Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain.”

- **The Pulpit Commentary** explains that Ahab had gone down to the Kishon with the crowd and that “the excitement of the ordeal was so intense that the king had barely tasted food all day.” Elijah now bids him eat; there is no longer cause for anxiety: the people are repentant and the men who brought a curse on the land are cut off. The “sound” of rain refers to signs and intimations understood only by the prophet — not yet audible to others. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-18.html)

- **Ellicott** detects “a touch of scorn” in Elijah’s words: Ahab, fresh from the horrible sight of the slaughter, is yet ready to feast and rejoice over the removal of the drought. “The king goes to revel, the prophet to pray.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keil & Delitzsch** note that once the occasion for the curse of drought was removed by the destruction of the idolatrous priests, the curse itself could be removed — but this was not to occur without the prophet’s prayer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-18.html)

---

## Verse 42

**Traditional Reading:** Ahab went up to eat and drink; Elijah climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees.

- **Ellicott** describes this posture as “one of prayer, but a peculiar attitude — distinct from the ordinary postures of standing and kneeling — which has been noted as existing still among the modern dervishes. Possibly it is characteristic of the vehement excitement of the moment, and of the impulsive nature of Elijah.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** says this was an unusual posture and shows that “the power in prayer resides in faith in the living God,” not in any particular bodily position. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Keathley (Bible.org)** comments with a touch of humour: “If some people assumed Elijah’s position for any length of time, they might not be able to get back on their feet. They would need a tow truck.” He adds that believers should assume whatever position helps them focus on the Lord. (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

---

## Verses 43–44

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah sent his servant to look toward the sea. The servant saw nothing. Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” On the seventh time the servant reported a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea. Elijah then told him to tell Ahab to prepare his chariot and go down before the rain stopped him.

- **Ellicott** remarks that “from this delay of the answer to prayer Elijah’s example became proverbial for intensity and perseverance in supplication (James 5:17).” He finds the contrast remarkable between the immediate answer in verse 38 and the long delay here: “The one was for the sake of the people; the other for some lesson — perhaps of humility and patience — to Elijah himself.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Guzik** calls this “stubbornly persistent prayer.” Elijah would not take “no” for an answer because he had confidence that God’s will was to send rain. “God’s promises are meant to incite us to prayer, not restrain it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

- **Gill** notes that the cloud was “either about the size or in the form of” a man’s hand, and that rain water comes out of the sea, being strained through the clouds and air to become fresh. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/18.htm)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** cites Conder’s observation: “Still in autumn the little cloud comes up like a man’s hand and swells till huge thunder pillars are piled black and high above the mountains.” The Pulpit also notes that the command to Ahab was urgent because after heavy rain the Kishon becomes an impassable swamp (cf. Judges 5:21). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-18.html)

---

## Verse 45

**Traditional Reading:** The sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall. Ahab rode away to Jezreel.

- **Ellicott** notes that Jezreel is mentioned here for the first time as a royal city. It stands in a position of strength and great beauty, supplied by unfailing springs, visible from Carmel, and commanding wide views over the plain. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keathley (Bible.org)** says the ultimate goal of the rain was “the removal of the spiritual drought in Israel. It was designed to turn sinners from seeking life apart from God.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

---

## Verse 46

**Traditional Reading:** The hand of the LORD came upon Elijah; he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.

- **Ellicott** describes this as “a striking reaction of enthusiastic thankfulness after the stern calmness of his whole attitude throughout the great controversy, and his silent earnestness of prayer.” He notes that such frenzied excitement would not have suited a Samuel, Elisha, or Isaiah, but “in the simple and enthusiastic warrior of God it is natural enough.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Gill** says “the hand of the Lord” gave Elijah more than common strength of body, as well as courage and fortitude of mind. The Targum renders it: “the spirit of strength from the Lord was with him.” Gill also notes that the run — about sixteen miles — showed Elijah’s humility: he was not elated by the wonders God had done, nor did he bear ill will to Ahab, but showed him honour as king. Some think he prudently stopped at the gate, avoiding Jezebel’s reach. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/18.htm)

- **Keil & Delitzsch** say Elijah ran before Ahab “not so much for the purpose of bringing the king to his residence unhurt, as to give him a proof of his humility, and thus deepen the impression already made upon his heart, and fortify him all the more against the strong temptations of his wife.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-18.html)

- **Guzik** simply calls it “Elijah’s amazing 14-mile cross-country run,” emphasising the supernatural enabling. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/)

---

## Denominational Distinctives (Where I Found Material)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic Reading (Enduring Word, Precept Austin)

- Emphasis falls on the supernatural fire (v. 38) as a “Pentecostal day for Israel,” and on persistent, expectant prayer for miracles (vv. 42–44). Precept Austin laments that unbelief hinders signs and wonders today (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary). Guzik stresses that the power of prayer lies in faith in the living God, not in technique, and that God’s promises should incite persistent prayer (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/).

### Evangelical (Bible.org / Keathley)

- Keathley frames the passage in terms of prayer as the divinely ordained means by which God’s promises are translated into performance, and emphasises that Elijah “was standing on the promises” — acting according to Scriptural revelation. He draws a strong application to cultural engagement: “God wants us to get involved in the issues of the day … earnest prayer for our nation and leaders … being informed, witnessing, voting.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/13-prayers-elijah-1-kings-1830-46)

### Anglican / Traditional Protestant (Ellicott)

- Ellicott gives measured historical-grammatical notes, treating Elijah’s character with some detachment (e.g., “frenzied excitement seems strange … in the simple and enthusiastic warrior of God it is natural enough”). He honestly engages the moral problem of the slaughter (v. 40) and offers a developmental view of ethics. He is careful to note that miracles are “granted unasked when it is seen by God’s wisdom to be needed.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/18.htm)

### Reformed / Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch)

- Keil & Delitzsch ground the execution of the prophets firmly in Deuteronomy’s legal requirements for the Old Testament kingdom, stressing the objective law rather than Elijah’s personal motives. They see Elijah’s run before Ahab as a calculated act to deepen conviction in the king’s heart. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-18.html)
